replacement: “The cellar was somewhere I had to go anyway, several times a day,” Smerdyakov drawled slowly. “A year ago I fell out of the garret in just the same way. It’s true enough that nobody can tell the day and the hour of a fit beforehand, but you can always have a foreboding.”

“That was simply out of affection and sincere devotion to you. I saw trouble coming in the house and wanted to spare you. But I wanted to spare myself even more. That’s why I told you to keep out of harm’s way, so you’d understand there’d be trouble in the house and stay at home to protect your father.”

“How could I say it straight out then? It was only my fear that made me speak at all, and you might have been angry too. I could well have been afraid that Dmitri Fyodorovitch would make a scene and take that money, since he thought of it as practically his own. But who could have told it would end in a murder like this? I thought he’d only take the three thousand under the master’s mattress, in the envelope, and look, he has murdered him. How could you have guessed it either, sir?”
“But at the time I thought you’d fully guessed,” Smerdyakov countered with a perfectly innocent air.
“Forgive me, I thought you were the same as me.”
“Out of plain simplicity. I’ve never faked a fit on purpose in my life. I only said it to boast to you. It was just foolish. I liked you so much then, and I was frank with you.”
“I’m very grateful for everything. Marfa Ignatyevna doesn’t forget me, and out of her kindness she gets me anything I need. Good people visit me every day.”
“I quite understand. And if you say nothing about that, I’ll say nothing about our conversation at the gate.”

His main feeling was relief that the murderer was Mitya and not Smerdyakov, though you would have expected the reverse. He did not want to analyze why, and in fact felt a real distaste for prying into his own feelings. He seemed to want to hurry up and forget something. Over the next few days he became convinced of Mitya’s guilt, as he learned how heavy the evidence against him was. Some of it came from unimportant people, Fenya and her mother for example, yet its effect was almost crushing. As for Perhotin, the people at the tavern and at Plotnikov’s shop, and the witnesses at Mokroe, their evidence looked conclusive. It was the details that did the damage. The secret of the knocks impressed the lawyers nearly as much as Grigory’s evidence about the open door. Grigory’s wife, Marfa, answering Ivan’s questions, declared that Smerdyakov had lain all night on the other side of the partition wall. “He was not three paces from our bed.” She was a sound sleeper, yet she had woken several times and heard him groaning. “He was groaning the whole time, groaning without a stop.”

But at that time something quite different was taking up most of his mind. On his return from Moscow he had given himself up, hopelessly, to a mad and consuming passion for Katerina Ivanovna. This is not the place to begin on that new passion of Ivan’s, which left its mark on the whole rest of his life. It would make the subject of another novel, which I may never write. But I cannot leave out one thing here. When Ivan, as I’ve already related, left Katerina Ivanovna with Alyosha and told him, “I am not keen on her,” it was an absolute lie. He loved her madly, though at times he hated her so much that he could have murdered her. Many causes helped to produce this feeling. Shattered by what had happened with Mitya, on Ivan’s return she had rushed to meet him as her one salvation. She had been hurt, insulted and humiliated in her feelings. And now back to her had come the man who had loved her so ardently before (oh! she knew that very well), and whose heart and intellect she thought far superior to her own. But the sternly virtuous girl did not surrender altogether to the man she loved, in spite of the Karamazov violence of his passions and the great fascination he had for her. At the same time she was constantly tormented by remorse for having deserted Mitya, and in moments of discord and violent anger (and there were plenty) she told Ivan so plainly. This was what he had meant when he told Alyosha, “lies upon lies.” There was, of course, much that was false in it, and that angered Ivan more than anything.... But of all this later.

“And it was true. There was no guessing about it. But didn’t you also suppose that what I wanted was just ‘one reptile devouring another’; that is, that Dmitri should kill father, and as soon as possible ... and that I myself was even ready to help it along?”

“Thanks,” snapped Ivan, and he left Alyosha and hurried on his way. From then on Alyosha noticed that Ivan clearly avoided him and even seemed to have taken a dislike to him, so much so that Alyosha stopped going to see him. Immediately after that meeting Ivan did not go home but went straight back to Smerdyakov.
“Nobody can hear anything. You’ve seen for yourself: there’s a passage.”
“I’m in perfect possession of all my faculties.”
“By ‘something else’ I meant that you, most likely, were very eager for your parent’s death as well.”
“I didn’t know what thoughts were in your mind then,” said Smerdyakov resentfully. “And so I stopped you at the gate then to sound you out on that very point.”
“Why, that very matter: whether you wanted your father murdered or not.”
“You know for a fact that it wasn’t me who murdered him. And I’d have thought a sensible man had no need to bring it up again.”

“As you already know, it was simply from fear. I was in such a position, shaking with fear, that I suspected everyone. I decided to sound you out too, because I thought: if you wanted the same as your brother, then the business was as good as settled, and I would be crushed like a fly as well.”
“What next! Come on, answer me, I insist: what was it ... what could I possibly have done to plant such a degrading suspicion in your mean soul?”

“What reason did you have? What about the inheritance?” said Smerdyakov sarcastically, and somehow vengefully. “After your parent’s death there was at least forty thousand to come to each of you, and very likely more. But if Fyodor Pavlovitch had married that lady, Agrafena Alexandrovna, she would have had all his capital transferred to her right after the wedding, for she has plenty of sense. Your parent wouldn’t have left the three of you two roubles. And were they far from a wedding, either? Not by a hair’s breadth. That lady had only to lift her little finger and he would have run after her to church with his tongue hanging out.”

“How could you help counting on him? If he killed him, he would lose all the rights of a nobleman, his rank and his property, and go off into exile. So his share of the inheritance would come to you and your brother Alexey Fyodorovitch in equal parts. You would each get not forty but sixty thousand. There’s no doubt at all that you counted on Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

“It was all that business of going to Tchermashnya. Why, you were meaning to go to Moscow, and you refused all your father’s pleading to go to Tchermashnya—and then at one foolish word from me you agreed at once! What reason did you have to agree to Tchermashnya? You went to Tchermashnya for no reason, simply on my word. That shows you must have expected something from me.”

“You didn’t? Then, as your father’s son, you should have had me hauled off to the lock-up and thrashed for what I said then ... or at the very least given me a punch in the face on the spot. But you weren’t the least bit angry, if you please. You at once acted, in the friendliest way, on my foolish word and went away. That was utterly absurd, for you ought to have stayed to save your parent’s life. How could I help drawing my conclusions?”

“In the ordinary occasions of life,” he said, in the same smug, sententious tone in which he had taunted Grigory and argued with him about religion at Fyodor Pavlovitch’s table, “in the ordinary occasions of life, blows on the face are forbidden by law nowadays, and people have given them up. But in exceptional occasions of life people still fly to blows, not only among us but all over the world, even in the fullest Republic of France, just as in the time of Adam and Eve. And they never will leave off. But you, even in an exceptional case, did not dare.”
